themes.theme: Equality impact assessment and the Public Sector Equality Duty
themes.definition: Assessment and monitoring of an AI tool's effects on people with protected characteristics, as a way of meeting the Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty (split from the starting code 'impact assessment').
themes.what_is_set_out: The EHRC checklist (UK216) is the core text: public bodies should identify how they, or others on their behalf, use AI; collect equality evidence; ask whether the proposed or existing AI 'cause, or could it cause, discrimination'; consider each protected characteristic and combinations of them (its example, per the coder note, compares younger Black and younger White men in facial recognition); keep records such as minutes; and monitor regularly because the PSED is 'an ‘ongoing duty’'. The EHRC also states that for public bodies in England 'there is no legal obligation to carry out an EIA', which is presented as a good way of showing the PSED was considered. Against this, UK099 says 'You must assess the equality impact of your project' before initiating, during and after implementation (coder note), and the DWP policy (UK190) says an Equality Analysis 'is required' where personal data on protected characteristics is processed by an AI tool. The Playbook (UK174) offers an equality impact assessment as 'one way to guard against bias' and restates compliance with the Equality Act and PSED, and UK136 asks procurers to assess how the PSED applies before procurement. [inference] The documents differ on whether a formal equality assessment is required (UK099, UK190) or optional (UK216, UK174), and none sets a level of disparity that would count as unacceptable.
themes.holders: Public bodies in England, and non-devolved and cross-border public bodies (UK216); 'you' (UK099, UK174); DWP users (UK190, nearest actor); central government departments and procurement teams (UK136).
themes.binding: The PSED is statutory; the EIA as a form is not legally required in England (UK216). UK099 uses 'must' in non-statutory guidance; DWP 'required' by departmental policy; others 'should', 'can', checklist steps. UK099 warns of unlawful discrimination and regulatory risk (coder note to 234); no sanctions are stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: at the start of decision-making; before initiating or procuring; during and after implementation; regularly as part of an ongoing duty; whenever protected-characteristic data is processed (UK190). Compared against: equality evidence; how other people are treated. Metric or threshold: differential treatment by protected characteristic, broken down by more than one characteristic where relevant, and how many people may be affected (coder note to 190); no threshold. Who: the public body; DWP users; not stated in several passages. What happens with the result: reduce risks; keep a record of how equality was considered; monitor third parties' compliance where they carry out the function.

themes.definition: Assessment of an AI tool's risks and impacts beyond data protection and equality (harm to individuals and society, misuse, misinformation, failure modes, AI-specific and organisational risks) and the risk-management processes built around it.
themes.what_is_set_out: Most documents ask for some form of risk or impact assessment, in different vocabularies. The Playbook (UK174) asks bodies to weigh positive and negative impacts, assess the risk of misinformation, and assess the potential for harm and misuse 'as part of the design of your project' (coder note), using 'a consistent risk rating methodology' such as OWASP. UK268 asks auditors whether the organisation has a risk analysis that 'explicitly considers the unique risks associated with AI', with harms mapped on standardised severity scales, horizon scanning, and attention to how interactions between models may amplify risk. UK099 makes considering knock-on effects on communities a 'must', asks whether 'the risks outweigh the expected benefits', and suggests harm-identification workshops at the planning stage; UK010 (Ofgem) expects regulated firms to 'identify, assess and prioritise AI-related risks' in proportion to likelihood, impact and materiality, and to assess failure modes including unintended consequences such as 'loss of skill base' (coder note). UK136 asks for an 'AI impact assessment' from the project design stage and the start of procurement, revisited at key decision points; UK071 lists DPIAs and Algorithmic Impact Assessments among planning activities; UK266, UK206, UK207 and UK139 pose risk questions or list risk processes, and DWP names two security risk management teams. Assessments are nearly always recommended rather than required, scoring methods appear only as examples, and what follows when a risk is judged too high is left to other rows.
themes.holders: 'You' or organisations; teams; stakeholders and users of AI (UK010); DWP's Digital Security Risk Management and Enterprise Security Risk Management teams (UK190); central government departments (UK136); organisations answering audit committees (UK266); AI developers and deployers in regulators' remits (UK139); those who build, deploy or use AI (UK207).
themes.binding: Non-statutory: 'should', imperatives, 'expected', questions. 'Must' in UK099 (253) and UK010 (288) guidance. Ofgem holds enforcement powers over licensees' regulatory obligations generally (see the legal-compliance theme) [inference: the risk assessment itself is not shown to be enforced].
themes.checks: Trigger: design and planning; before use; start of procurement and key decision points; regularly; when scaling from pilot. Compared against: severity scales; likelihood and impact; the Playbook's principles; expected benefits. Metric or threshold: likelihood, impact, severity, materiality; OWASP as an example method; an 'Impact Assessment Score' or risk heatmap as example outputs (UK071 coder note); no thresholds. Who: mostly not stated; named DWP risk teams. What happens with the result: mitigation measures; risk register; mitigations tested for effectiveness (UK174, 026).

themes.definition: Requirements to assess and track the energy, water, carbon and material footprint of an AI tool and weigh it against the tool's benefits.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) recommends assessing the environmental impact of training or deploying a system 'before commencing development', weighing benefits against energy use (coder note). UK268 lists 'Assess and document energy use, water consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions where possible' as an expected control. UK099 gives the fullest treatment: monitor electricity, water, raw materials and e-waste across the life cycle, choose KPIs that can be tracked over time (named examples: CO2e, kWh, FLOPs per watt, litres of water), prefer smaller models for specific tasks, and document decisions about trade-offs and the governance used. AI_Insights folds environmental impact into a continual review of running costs and technical decisions. All are recommendations; there are no thresholds and no reporting duty.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099); not stated (UK268); teams running generative AI (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Non-binding: imperatives, 'should', 'where possible'. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before development; across the life cycle; continually. Compared against: the benefits of the tool; less energy-intensive options. Metric or threshold: energy, water, greenhouse gas emissions (CO2e), compute efficiency; no thresholds. Who: 'you'; not stated. What happens with the result: trade-off decisions documented; the solution iterated.

themes.theme: Security by design, access control and data-leakage protection
themes.definition: Security requirements on AI tools in use: compliance with the government's Secure by Design principles, access controls, protection of official and personal data from leakage, secure development and production environments, and threat monitoring.
themes.what_is_set_out: Secure by Design is the one security requirement stated as mandatory policy: the Playbook (UK174) says a service 'must comply with the government’s Secure by Design principles before it can be deployed', UK099 repeats that new AI services must comply, and UK266 reports the principles as mandatory for central government (coder note to 630). The Playbook also forbids entering official information into public AI applications unless it is published or cleared for publication, says a model should only access data its user may access, asks for enterprise access controls to be reviewed before deployment and continually, and places responsibility for keeping a self-hosted model 'secure and up to date' on the body. AI_Insights adds that before enabling an integrated AI service (its examples include Microsoft 365 Copilot, per the coder note to 435) 'you must understand what data is visible to integrated AI services'; it asks for sandboxing and anonymisation, tighter access permissions before migrating shared drives into such environments, security at all stages of AI-enabled reviews, no secrets in coding-assistant development environments, and a production environment insulated from development changes. UK268, UK010 (Ofgem), UK071, NAO, UK206, UK139 and UK266 add access controls and encryption, cyber risk management, ongoing threat monitoring by cyber security teams, and audit-committee questions about AI-specific threats and legacy interfaces. Apart from Secure by Design, all of this is recommendation, and the frequent 'must' in guidance carries no stated consequence.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099, AI_Insights); staff using public AI applications (UK174); developers and 'you as risk owner' (AI_Insights); KIM professionals; stakeholders (UK010); cyber security teams (UK010); NAO; 'your organisation' (UK206); AI developers and deployers encouraged by regulators (UK139); the organisation answering audit committees (UK266).
themes.binding: Secure by Design is mandatory by policy (UK174, UK099; reported as mandatory in UK266); the ban on entering official information into public AI tools is a 'must not' in non-statutory guidance (UK174, 069); otherwise 'should', 'must' in guidance, 'can', questions. Consequence: UK174 implies the service cannot be deployed until compliant [inference from 'before it can be deployed'].
themes.checks: Trigger: before deployment; before enabling an integrated AI service; before migrating content; continually. Compared against: Secure by Design principles; the organisation's data security policies; the user's own access permissions. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: 'you'; cyber security teams; the risk owner. What happens with the result: deployment only after compliance (UK174); controls applied; access tightened.

themes.definition: Tests that deliberately try to make an AI tool fail (red teaming, jailbreaks, prompt injection, malicious or edge-case inputs, checks for poisoned data or models) in order to find vulnerabilities and failure modes.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) recommends red teaming and recording 'how your model behaves when it encounters unexpected and anomalous scenarios', and security testing as one of the safeguards for generative AI. UK268 lists regular vulnerability testing ('red teaming'), testing of security mitigations, and attention to backdoors in external or open-source models and to data poisoning. UK099 asks for 'rigorous testing to identify potential failure modes', including adversarial models that generate prompts (coder note), and supply-chain checks because poisoned models often come from fine-tuned pre-trained ones. UK071 is the most concrete for LLMs: attempt to bypass filters or jailbreak the model, 'Break its fact-checking' with deliberately incorrect prompts, and simulate malicious and edge-case inputs, with example targets such as none of 50 adversarial prompts yielding unsafe output and an adversarial failure rate below 2% (coder notes). AI_Insights makes attack-surface testing 'mandatory prior to any model change', says 'Constant vigilance is required' against new jailbreak techniques, and lists red-team testing as required for Critical-risk LLM uses. All of this is non-binding, and thresholds appear only as examples.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099); not stated (UK268); the team (UK071); 'we' and development teams (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Non-binding: imperatives, 'should', 'possible control'; 'mandatory', 'required' and 'must' within guidance (AI_Insights). No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: during development; regularly; before any model change; continually. Compared against: expected safe behaviour; known vulnerabilities and attack techniques. Metric or threshold: UK071 examples (0 of 50 adversarial prompts unsafe; adversarial failure rate below 2%); otherwise not stated. Who: not stated; the team. What happens with the result: patch and retest (UK071 coder note); update defences (UK268).

themes.theme: Filtering and constraining prompts and outputs
themes.definition: Automated guardrails on what goes into and comes out of a generative AI tool: input safeguards, content filters, sanitising of responses, schema validation and prompt instructions that constrain answers.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) recommends content filtering and validation checks so that responses are accurate and do not leak data (coder note), says a body 'can' add content filters to sanitise prompts and responses, and states in a recommendations box that responses with external links 'must be filtered to remove malicious URLs'. UK099 says off-the-shelf generative tools 'will likely need' pre- and post-prompt filters, and UK268 lists content filters to prevent disclosure of sensitive information. UK071 asks teams to validate prompts and inputs, block harmful requests and enforce schema validation for structured outputs. AI_Insights uses the strongest wording: 'All communicated data must be monitored and evaluated without exception', responses 'must be examined and sanitised before return' (applying to internal as well as external systems, per coder note), prompts should ensure queries 'do no harm', the model should be told how to respond when an answer cannot be found so as to avoid hallucination, and higher-risk applications should layer content filtering and output auditing on top of prompt engineering. These filters are automated checks on outputs, but no document says how accurate the filters must be or how they are themselves tested.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099, AI_Insights); not stated (UK268, UK071, and several AI_Insights passages; nearest those building LLM systems).
themes.binding: Non-binding guidance. 'Must' in a UK174 recommendations box (075) and in AI_Insights (481, 488, 546) without stated force; 'can', 'should', 'will likely need' elsewhere.
themes.checks: Trigger: every input and every response before it is returned. Compared against: harmful-content policies, lists of malicious URLs, output schemas, the target domain. Metric or threshold: not stated; UK071 gives examples such as adversarial prompts failing less than 1% of the time (coder note to 357). Who: not stated (automated). What happens with the result: block, filter or sanitise; a fallback response when no answer is found.

themes.theme: AI used by others against the public body (edge cases)
themes.definition: Passages, mostly flagged by the coders as edge cases, about protecting a public body's services from AI used by outsiders: manipulated images or video, AI-generated correspondence and content, AI-enabled cyber attack and AI-driven increases in workload.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says, with 'must', that services receiving images or video need mechanisms 'to detect if the content has been manipulated by AI', and asks bodies to consider the effect of AI-generated correspondence on decisions (areas named in the coder note include procurement, recruitment and FOI requests), to treat incoming digital content as possibly unreliable, and to expect more cyber attacks. UK010 (Ofgem) asks stakeholders to widen threat intelligence to include AI; UK268 mentions provenance detection to help identify AI-generated material; UK266 asks audit committees whether organisations monitor the risk that external uses of AI may 'dramatically increase the workload'. These passages concern AI used against the body rather than the body's own AI tool, so they sit at the edge of the framework's object; they are kept together here so that the reader can decide whether to include them.
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174); not stated (UK268); stakeholders (UK010); the organisation and its audit committee (UK266).
themes.binding: 'Must' in UK174 (076) non-statutory guidance; 'should', 'need to' and questions elsewhere. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: when building services that receive digital content; ongoing threat monitoring. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: 'you'; stakeholders; not stated. What happens with the result: not stated.

themes.theme: Quality of training, input, retrieval and synthetic data
themes.definition: Checks on the data an AI tool learns from or works on: provenance, representativeness, completeness, separation of training and test sets, poisoning, the validity of synthetic data, and the accuracy of inputs that users supply.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268 lists expected controls: assess the provenance of web-scraped or synthetic training data, test whether key population characteristics are represented in training, test and validation data, keep data splits representative, consider data poisoning, validate synthetic data and have humans verify LLM-generated data 'where feasible'. UK071 gives an operational rule ('If one group is less than 15% of the dataset, apply sampling or weighting and document the decision') with example metrics such as a missing-value rate of 1% or less (coder note), and UK099 says 'All civil servants have a responsibility' for data quality and fitness for purpose. The DWP policy (UK190) requires users and suppliers to 'ensure to the best of their ability' that data they give AI tools is accurate. AI_Insights says synthetic data 'must be subject to the same evaluations as real-world data', asks for checks that synthetic data has not biased a model towards artificial patterns, for knowledge bases to be updated with verified information, and for seed corpora that cover edge cases; UK136 asks for data discovery before going to market and, where that is hard, a supplier data check written into the tender. The ATRS (UK087) asks bodies to disclose completeness and representativeness, and UK266 asks whether data are assessed for fitness for purpose before training or deployment; thresholds are rare and appear only as examples.
themes.holders: Not stated, nearest the organisation (UK268); the team (UK071); all civil servants, data stewards (UK099); users and suppliers (UK190); stakeholders (UK010); 'we' or 'you' (AI_Insights); organisations (UK206); central government departments, data architects and suppliers (UK136); the organisation completing the ATRS record; the organisation answering audit committees (UK266).
themes.binding: DWP 'must' by departmental policy; UK099 'have a responsibility'; AI_Insights 'must' in guidance; expected controls and 'should' elsewhere. No consequences stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: before training, procurement or deployment; on generating synthetic data; on regular knowledge-base updates; ongoing monitoring of input data (UK268). Compared against: the target population; real-world distributions; IP and data protection requirements; agreed fairness and robustness criteria (UK071, 317). Metric or threshold: representativeness (UK071's 15% example), missing values, distribution similarity; mostly not stated. Who: varied, often not stated. What happens with the result: sampling or weighting with the decision documented; flaws addressed before going to market or a plan for them (UK136).

themes.theme: User research, usability, accessibility and inclusion
themes.definition: Checks carried out with real users: user research to understand needs and set baselines, usability and acceptance testing, accessibility testing, and making sure groups are not excluded.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Playbook (UK174) says, with 'must', that bodies understand 'people’s needs and priorities by conducting user research and engaging with the public as appropriate', and recommends testing output accuracy and relevance with a sample of users, using early research to set a baseline of metrics, building usability testing into monitoring to understand drift through user behaviour, and checking whether any users are excluded. UK099 asks for non-digital alternatives 'where possible' and restates that public sector websites and applications must meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines unless exempt (coder note); UK071 asks for testing against WCAG 2.2 AA to help meet the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations, pilots with representative users on real tasks, and tests of whether non-technical users can tell when the AI is wrong. UK268 asks for end users to be involved in acceptance testing. UK099 also requires protection for research participants, which concerns the research process rather than the AI tool (the coder flagged this as a scope doubt).
themes.holders: 'You' (UK174, UK099); user researchers with analytical colleagues (UK174); the team and third-party researchers (UK099); not stated, nearest the team (UK071, UK268).
themes.binding: UK174 'must' (011) in non-statutory guidance; the accessibility duty is stated as 'must' with exemptions (UK099, 239) and linked to the accessibility regulations (UK071); otherwise 'should', good practice, core practice.
themes.checks: Trigger: early, before building; during development; pilot or beta phase; ongoing. Compared against: users' judgement; WCAG 2.2 AA; a baseline of metrics. Metric or threshold: accuracy and relevance as judged by users; usability; accessibility conformance; UK071 example metrics; otherwise not stated. Who: user researchers; the team; representative users. What happens with the result: baseline for measuring outcomes; identifying excluded groups and why.
